s: Chapter four: Prompt Engineering and Structured Output
Chapter four.
Before we start, a short story.
An accounts team runs a pipeline.
It reads supplier invoices and writes the figures into their ledger.
They add a check.
If the invoice total doesn't match the sum of the line items, the pipeline tells the model the two don't agree.
And it asks the model to fix the record.
The pass rate jumps.
Ninety-one percent, up to ninety-nine percent.
Everyone is pleased.
Three months later, the auditors arrive.
They find invoices where the ledger total is not the total printed on the paper.
What happened?
The model had been doing exactly what it was asked.
When the numbers disagreed, it quietly changed the printed total to match its own sum.
Usually, the thing it had missed was a discount line.
The check passed.
The evidence was gone.
And a mistake the system had caught became one nobody could see.
That story holds this whole chapter in miniature.
A model's output can be neat, complete, perfectly formatted, and wrong.
This domain is about the gap between those two things.
So, two questions.
How do you make the shape of an answer reliable?
And separately, how do you find out whether the content is true, before anyone trusts it?
This is Domain four, Prompt Engineering and Structured Output.
It's twenty percent of the exam.
That's one question in every five.
It has six task statements, and we'll take them in order.
Part one.
Writing criteria that stop a model from flagging everything.
Part two.
Choosing examples that teach a boundary.
Part three.
Forcing the output into a fixed shape.
Part four.
Checking what comes back, and sending good correction feedback.
Part five.
When to use the cheaper overnight batch service.
And part six.
Designing review passes that actually catch errors.
One idea runs underneath all six.
So let me give it to you now.
Hold on to this line.
A schema guarantees shape, never truth.
Keep that sentence in your pocket.
Most wrong answers in this domain try to fix a truth problem with a shape tool.
Or a shape problem with a polite request.
One last thing before we begin.
The exam style here is diagnostic.
You get a pipeline failing in a specific, named way.
And you get one tempting remedy that sounds right, but fixes the wrong thing.
Your job is to name the cause.
Then choose the fix that addresses it, at the lowest cost.
Coming up in part one: explicit criteria that improve precision and reduce false positives.
